title: What's the nastiest bug AI wrote into a backtest that still looked profitable?
author: Alphanet_dogwalker
selftext:
The syntax errors are easy to notice. I'm more interested in the ones where the code runs, the chart looks great, and the mistake only shows up when you inspect individual trades.

For example: a signal uses the candle's closing price, but the simulated entry happens earlier in that candle. Or several overlapping positions each get to spend the same available cash. Those are hypothetical examples, not results from a bot I'm running.

If you've caught one of these in AI-assisted code, what was the mistake and what finally exposed it? A tiny code snippet or one broken trade would be more useful than the whole strategy.

Also interested in whether asking the model to review its own code caught it, or whether you needed a separate check

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body:
the one that got me wasn't in the backtest, it was in the bookkeeping that fed it, and it's the same shape as your examples: code runs, totals look plausible, only the individual rows are wrong.

a spread's symbol packs two expiry dates. the code took the first date it matched as the expiry, which is the short leg. so every diagonal got filed as an expired, dead position the day its short leg died, while the long leg was still live and moving. nobody noticed for a week because the dead positions were small and the totals still added up to something believable.

the second one I've hit is the target touch. the target sits inside the bar's range, so the sim fills it at the target price, when in reality the wick kissed it once with no size there. that one bug flatters any strategy with a target.

both were found the way you describe: opening ten random trades by hand and reading them like a stranger would.

replies.author: Alphanet_dogwalker
replies.body:
The diagonal one is nasty. Everything adds up, except you're still holding something the system thinks is dead.  
  
What did you end up doing about the target fills? Did you go down to trade data or use a stricter fill rule? curious how much of the apparent edge survived that fix

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: stricter rule, not trade data. everything fills at the worst side of the quote, buys at the ask and sells at the bid. I never measured how much apparent edge that ate across the whole fleet, which is a fair thing to go count.

replies.author: Alphanet_dogwalker
replies.body: That accounts for the spread. I'd still separate the fill price from whether the order could fill at all. If a target touch still triggers the exit charging the spread can leave the original problem in there. I'd check whether those exits had an executable quote for the required size at that moment

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: fair, those are two different questions, and size is the part almost nobody models. it's part of why I built Quantradin to fill paper options at the live bid and ask rather than on a touch, though it doesn't model depth either. free, quantradin.com.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body:
A common one that runs clean and looks great: joining event data on the wrong date. For example, an AI-written backtest merges an earnings result (or CPI print) onto price bars by the fiscal period end date or the calendar date, not the actual release timestamp. The strategy then "knows" the surprise hours or weeks before the market did, so entries look prescient. The code has no errors, the equity curve is smooth, and it only shows up when you pull one trade and compare its entry time against the real release time.

What exposed it: taking a single winning trade and asking "when was this information publicly knowable?", then comparing that timestamp against the entry bar. A DST slip between UTC and exchange time creates the same kind of leak on a smaller scale.

On self-review: asking the same model to check its own code mostly missed it, since the logic reads as reasonable. What worked was a separate test that asserts every feature's availability timestamp is earlier than the bar it's used on. That's why we keep release timestamps explicit in EventTrader at Cymetica. It makes that assertion possible to write. [https://claude.ai/artifact/VuwYE2KYrtzMdwyEpvA9wH](https://claude.ai/artifact/VuwYE2KYrtzMdwyEpvA9wH)

replies.author: Alphanet_dogwalker
replies.body:
>The other sneaky version is the right release timestamp attached to a revised value. The timing check passes, but it's still a number nobody had on the day. I'd want the original release and later revisions stored separately. Otherwise a perfectly sensible as-of join can still leak future information
